result: Pathogenic HTT Q138 aggregates severely impair clathrin-coated structure (CCS) movement and directionality in Drosophila hemocytes and mammalian cells. Live cell imaging with PIV analysis demonstrated that while WT/HTT Q15 cells show centripetal CCS movement with defined speeds, HTT Q138 cells exhibit little to no CCS movement with negligible radial speed and loss of directional movement. This was accompanied by reduced mBSA internalization and was conserved across cell types.
evaluation: Claims C21, C33-C38 provide converging evidence from multiple experimental approaches (kymographs, PIV analysis, ligand uptake assays) across different cell types (Drosophila hemocytes, HEK293T, SH-SY5Y) demonstrating impaired CCS dynamics in HTT Q138. The quantitative PIV analysis and visual data in Figures 1 and supplementary figures provide strong support.

result: HTT Q138 aggregates sequester actin and Arp2/3 complex components, leading to disrupted actin dynamics. Actin-GFP was sequestered in HTT Q138 aggregates, and cells showed dramatic alterations in actin dynamics with reduced filopodia number and length, increased cortical actin thickness and intensity, reduced barbed-end actin incorporation, and reduced actin flow. Arp3 was significantly enriched within HTT Q138 aggregates.
evaluation: Claims C22, C43-C47, C50 are supported by multiple complementary assays including co-localization studies (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), live imaging of actin dynamics (Figure 2C-E), barbed-end labeling (Figure 2H-I), cortical actin measurements (Figure 2F-G), PIV analysis of actin flow (Figure 2J), and Arp3 sequestration data (Figure 3A). The convergence of multiple independent measurements strengthens the conclusion.

result: Pharmacological or genetic disruption of actin polymerization phenocopies HTT Q138-induced CCS defects. Treatment with LatA or CytoD, knockdown of Arp3 or Profilin, or chemical inhibition of Formin all resulted in stalled CCS movement, loss of directionality, and reduced filopodia formation similar to HTT Q138 cells.
evaluation: Claims C41-C42, C51-C54 demonstrate that multiple independent perturbations of actin polymerization machinery produce similar phenotypes to HTT Q138, supported by kymographs, PIV analysis, and filopodia quantification (Figures 2A-B, 3B-D, supplementary figures). This provides strong evidence that actin dysfunction is central to the HTT Q138 phenotype.

result: Overexpression of Arp3, Hip1, or the chaperone Mrj partially rescues CCS movement defects and neurodegeneration caused by pathogenic Huntingtin. Co-expression of these proteins with HTT Q138 restored CCS movement, directionality, and filopodia formation in hemocytes, and rescued neurodegeneration in Drosophila eyes expressing HTT Q127.
evaluation: Claims C23, C64, C69, C76-C77 are supported by live imaging data showing restored CCS dynamics (Figure 4A-D), filopodia quantification (Figure 4E), and eye phenotype rescue (Figure 4F). The rescue experiments provide strong evidence for the mechanistic role of these proteins. However, the rescues are described as 'partial,' which appropriately acknowledges incomplete restoration.

result: Hip1 knockdown in wild-type hemocytes impairs CCS movement, speed, and directionality.
evaluation: Claim C70 is supported by kymograph and PIV analysis data (Figure 4C, C', C'') showing that Hip1 knockdown phenocopies aspects of HTT Q138, providing loss-of-function evidence complementing the overexpression rescue experiments.

result: HTT Q138 expressing cells display increased cellular stiffness in an actin-dependent manner, which can be rescued by overexpression of Hip1 or Mrj or by LatA treatment. AFM measurements showed HTT Q138 cells had higher Young's modulus than WT cells, and this stiffness was partially rescued by Hip1 or Mrj overexpression. Treatment with CK666 or LatA decreased cellular stiffness.
evaluation: Claims C25, C78-C81 are supported by AFM nanoindentation measurements (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 3). The data show consistent increases in Young's modulus with HTT Q138 and rescue with actin-modulating interventions. The methodology appears sound with appropriate controls and statistical analysis.

result: Transient LatA treatment of HTT Q138 cells restores CCS movement at intermediate time points.
evaluation: Claims C26, C82 are supported by kymograph data (Figure 5B) showing that brief LatA treatment can restore CCS movement in HTT Q138 cells. This elegant experiment supports the 'Goldilocks' hypothesis that CCS movement requires an intermediate, dynamic actin state.

result: TDP-43 aggregates cause defective CME and stalled CCS movement similar to HTT Q138. Among multiple pathogenic aggregates tested (Aβ42, FUS, αSynA30P, αSynA53T, TDP-43), only TDP-43 showed significant reduction in CCS movement with complete stalling, reduced mean instantaneous velocities, reduced mBSA uptake, and compromised clathrin recovery in FRAP experiments.
evaluation: Claims C27, C83-C87 are supported by systematic comparison across multiple aggregating proteins using kymographs, particle tracking, velocity analysis (Figure 6A-C), mBSA uptake (Figure 6D), and FRAP (Figure 6—figure supplement 1). The specificity of the TDP-43 phenotype strengthens the conclusion that not all aggregates affect CME through the same mechanism.

result: TDP-43 aggregates dramatically reduce filopodia formation and actin dynamics. TDP-43 expressing cells showed reduced filopodia number, length, and lifetime, as well as reduced actin flow, while other aggregates (Aβ42, FUS, αSyn mutants) had no significant effect.
evaluation: Claims C88-C90 are supported by quantitative analysis of filopodia parameters (Figure 7A-D) and PIV analysis of actin flow (Figure 7E). The specificity for TDP-43 parallels the CCS movement data, providing consistent evidence for a shared mechanism between HTT Q138 and TDP-43.

result: TDP-43 aggregates increase cellular stiffness similar to HTT Q138, while other pathogenic aggregates do not. AFM measurements showed that cells with Aβ42, FUS R521C, αSynA30P, or αSynA53T aggregates had Young's modulus similar to WT, while TDP-43 cells showed increased stiffness comparable to HTT Q138.
evaluation: Claims C91-C92, C94 are supported by AFM data (Figure 8A) showing selective stiffness increases only with HTT Q138 and TDP-43. This provides strong evidence for a direct correlation between altered actin dynamics, CME defects, and cellular stiffness for these specific aggregates.

result: FRAP analysis reveals compromised clathrin light chain exchange in HTT Q138 cells and upon actin perturbation, but not in microtubule disruption. Recovery of Clc-GFP fluorescence was severely compromised in HTT Q138, Profilin knockdown, and LatA treatment, while microtubule organization remained unchanged in HTT Q138 cells.
evaluation: Claims C55-C57 are supported by FRAP data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and live imaging of microtubules (Figure 3—videos 1-2). The FRAP experiments provide mechanistic insight into how HTT Q138 affects clathrin dynamics, and the microtubule data appropriately rule out this cytoskeletal component.

result: Myosin VI knockdown impairs CCS movement but does not affect actin dynamics or filopodia formation.
evaluation: Claims C62-C63 are supported by kymograph data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—video 3-4) showing that Myosin VI affects CCS movement independently of actin dynamics. This helps dissect the relative contributions of different motor proteins versus actin organization.

result: The study demonstrates that specific pathogenic aggregates (HTT Q138 and TDP-43) alter cellular physical properties by impacting actin dynamics and CME, and that rescuing these functions can reduce neurotoxicity. The mechanical response can serve as a biomarker for actin-mediated altered cell behavior, and toxicity may result from reorganization of proteins and cellular pathways.
evaluation: Claims C93, C95-C98 represent the major conclusions synthesizing the experimental findings. These are well-supported by the convergence of CCS dynamics, actin organization, stiffness measurements, and rescue experiments across the manuscript. The biomarker claim (C96) is appropriately framed as a conclusion from the AFM data.

result: The extent of CCS and actin defects varies by aggregate type, with HTT Q138 and TDP-43 causing the most severe effects. The branching function of Arp2/3 is essential for CME, and altered Arp2/3 function by HTT Q138 may be a mechanism of CME inhibition in Huntington's disease.
evaluation: Claims C99-C103 synthesize the comparative analysis across aggregates and the Arp2/3 mechanistic data. The specificity of effects is well-documented (Figures 6-8), and the Arp2/3 mechanism is supported by sequestration data, knockdown/inhibition experiments, and rescue experiments. Claim C103 appropriately uses 'may be' to indicate this is one possible mechanism.

result: Overexpressing Hip1 and Arp2/3 ameliorates Huntingtin aggregate-induced loss of function. Previous work shows tight correlation between Hip1R/Arp2/3 availability and endocytic efficiency, with Hip1R distribution regulating recruitment of Arp2/3 complexes.
evaluation: Claim C105 is supported by the rescue experiments in the current study (Figure 4, Figure 8B). Claims C106-C107 cite prior work (Akamatsu et al., 2020) to provide mechanistic context. The integration of current and prior findings is appropriate.

result: The ratio of branching to capping proteins regulates actin network stiffness, with stiffness increasing as either concentration increases. Network stiffness depends on balancing branching and capping, and alterations may affect stiffness and endocytic efficiency.
evaluation: Claims C108-C110 cite prior in vitro work (Pujol et al., 2012) to provide theoretical framework for interpreting the stiffness results. The citation appears accurate and the interpretation (C110) is reasonable based on the cited work and current findings.

result: Clathrin exchange between membrane-associated and soluble pools is compromised in HTT Q138 and TDP-43 aggregates.
evaluation: Claim C111 cites prior FRAP studies (Wu et al., 2001; 2003) establishing clathrin exchange. Claim C112 interprets the current FRAP data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 6—figure supplement 1) in this context. The conclusion is well-supported by the FRAP experiments.

result: CME changes in HTT Q138 and TDP-43 may be actin-dependent, whereas other aggregates may use different mechanisms. Prior work showed that loss of CME in embryonic stem cells alters actin organization and increases stiffness, consistent with the current findings linking mechanical response to altered actin organization in HTT Q138 and TDP-43.
evaluation: Claim C113 is a reasonable interpretation of the aggregate comparison data. Claim C114 cites prior work from the authors' lab (Mote et al., 2020). Claim C115 synthesizes current AFM and actin dynamics data. The logic connecting these claims is sound.

result: The branched actin network generates force for cellular processes including endocytosis, and a 'Goldilocks' intermediate dynamic state is required for efficient CME—neither too soft nor too stiff.
evaluation: Claim C116 cites prior work on actin force generation (Goode et al., 2015; Lacy et al., 2018; Planade et al., 2019). Claim C117 represents a key conceptual conclusion from the stiffness and rescue experiments, particularly the transient LatA treatment (Figure 5B). This 'Goldilocks' model is well-supported by the data.

result: Rescue of Huntingtin-driven neurodegeneration by actin binding protein overexpression indicates that actin cytoskeleton remodeling contributes largely to aggregate-driven neurotoxicity. The conservation of CCS movement phenotypes across cell types and organisms suggests potential for screening molecular candidates for Huntington's disease.
evaluation: Claim C118 is supported by the eye rescue experiments (Figure 4F) combined with the mechanistic data on actin. Claim C119 is supported by the conservation of phenotypes across Drosophila hemocytes, HEK293T, and SH-SY5Y cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2). Both conclusions are well-justified.

result: Background claims establishing prior knowledge about Huntington's disease, CME, actin biology, and related neurodegenerative disorders.
evaluation: These claims (C1-C20, C29-C32, C39-C40, C48-C49, C58-C61, C65-C68, C71-C75, C104, C120-C125) cite published literature to establish context and prior knowledge. The citations appear appropriate and accurately represent the cited work based on the claims made.
